lessons.title: Fixing and Protecting Charcoal Drawings
lessons.body:
Charcoal smudges easily, so fixing your drawing is the first step to protect your work. You need a workable fixative spray, such as Krylon Workable Fixatif or a local equivalent like Bostik fixative. Work outdoors or in a well-ventilated area. Hold the can 30 cm from the drawing and spray in light, even passesâleft to right, then top to bottom. Apply 2-3 thin coats, waiting 10 minutes between coats. Do not overspray, or the charcoal will darken and lose its texture. For a cheaper alternative, you can use hairspray, but test it first on a scrap piece because some hairsprays yellow over time.

After fixing, let the drawing dry for at least 30 minutes. To further protect it, place a sheet of glassine paper or acid-free tissue over the surface before storing or framing. Glassine is available at art supply shops in cities like Nairobi, Lagos, or Johannesburg. If you cannot find glassine, use a clean sheet of newsprint, but avoid newspaper because the ink can transfer.

For drawings that will be handled often, consider mounting them on a rigid board. Use acid-free double-sided tape or wheat starch paste to attach the drawing to a piece of acid-free mat board. This prevents creases and tears. If you plan to sell your work, always fix and mount it before delivery. A well-protected drawing shows professionalism and increases its value.

Store fixed drawings flat in a portfolio or between two pieces of cardboard. Keep them away from moisture and direct sunlight. In humid regions like coastal West Africa, add silica gel packets to your storage box to prevent mold. Check your drawings every few months for signs of smudging or foxing (brown spots). If you see smudges, you can lightly erase them with a kneaded eraser before re-fixing. Remember, fixing is not permanent; it can be reactivated by moisture, so handle with care.

lessons.title: Matting and Framing Charcoal Art
lessons.body:
Matting and framing protect your charcoal drawing and make it ready to hang or sell. You will need a mat board (acid-free, 4-ply), a backing board, a frame, and glass or acrylic glazing. For a standard 30x40 cm drawing, cut your mat board to 40x50 cm. The opening (window) should be 2 cm smaller than your drawing on each side, so the mat overlaps the edges. Use a utility knife and a metal ruler to cut the mat. Practice on scrap first.

Place your drawing face up on the backing board. Center it, then place the mat over it. Use acid-free linen tape to hinge the drawing to the backing board at the top edge only. This allows the paper to expand and contract with humidity. Do not tape all sides, or the paper will buckle. For a professional look, add a second mat (a double mat) with a contrasting color.

Choose glazing carefully. Glass is scratch-resistant but heavy and breakable. Acrylic (Plexiglas) is lighter and safer for shipping, but it scratches easily and can build static that attracts charcoal dust. If using glass, make sure it does not touch the drawingâuse a mat or spacers to create a gap. For charcoal, always use glazing; without it, the drawing will smudge. In dusty environments, seal the back of the frame with kraft paper or framing tape to keep out insects and dust.

Frames can be bought ready-made or custom-made by local carpenters. In many African cities, you can find affordable wooden frames at markets like Balogun in Lagos or Kariakoo in Dar es Salaam. Paint or stain the frame to match your artwork. For a rustic look, use reclaimed wood. Attach hanging hardwareâD-rings and wireâto the back of the frame. Use two D-rings, one on each side, about one-third from the top. String the wire between them, leaving enough slack to hang on a hook. Finally, clean the glazing with a soft cloth and glass cleaner before final assembly. Your framed charcoal art is now ready to display.

lessons.title: Photographing Charcoal Art
lessons.body:
Good photographs help you sell your charcoal art online or submit to exhibitions. You do not need an expensive camera; a smartphone with at least 12 megapixels works. Use natural daylightâshoot outdoors on a cloudy day or in a room with a large window, but avoid direct sunlight because it creates harsh shadows. Place your drawing on a neutral background, like a white or grey wall or a large sheet of paper. If the drawing is framed behind glass, remove it from the frame to avoid reflections. If you must shoot through glass, tilt the frame slightly and position yourself so reflections fall away.

Set your camera to the highest resolution and use a grid or level to keep the drawing straight. Fill the frame with the artwork, leaving a small border. Use a tripod or stack of books to steady your phone. For sharp focus, tap the screen on the drawing. If your phone has a manual mode, set ISO to 100 and shutter speed to 1/125 second. Use a remote shutter or the timer to avoid shake. Take multiple shotsâat least 5âand bracket exposures (one normal, one brighter, one darker).

After shooting, edit the photos on your phone using free apps like Snapseed or Lightroom Mobile. Adjust brightness, contrast, and white balance to match the original. Crop to straighten the edges. Do not over-edit; charcoal has subtle tones. Save as high-quality JPEG or PNG. For online sales, resize to 1500 pixels on the longest side and 72 dpi for web, but keep a high-resolution version (300 dpi) for printing. Name your files clearly, e.g., 'charcoal_baobab_2024.jpg'.

If you plan to print reproductions, consider scanning your drawing with a flatbed scanner at 300-600 dpi. Scanners capture fine details without glare. Many print shops in African cities offer scanning services for a small fee. For video, record a slow pan across the drawing to show texture. Use a tripod and good lighting. Post your photos on social media with relevant hashtags like #AfricanArt #CharcoalDrawing. Good photography can increase your sales by 50% or more.

lessons.title: Selling and Exhibiting Charcoal Art
lessons.body:
To sell your charcoal art, you need to find the right audience. Start locally: cafes, hotels, and art galleries in your city often display local artists. In Nairobi, try the GoDown Arts Centre; in Accra, the Nubuke Foundation; in Cape Town, the Zeitz MOCAA. Approach them with a portfolio of 5-10 framed pieces. Offer to hang your work on consignmentâthey take 30-50% commission. Set a fair price: calculate your materials (charcoal, paper, frame) plus 3-5 times your hourly rate. For a 30x40 cm framed drawing, a typical price in Africa ranges from $50 to $300, depending on your reputation.

Online platforms expand your reach. Use Instagram, Facebook Marketplace, or Etsy. Post high-quality photos and write a short story about each piece. Include dimensions, materials, and price. For shipping, use rigid tubes or flat boxes with bubble wrap. Charge shipping separately. In Africa, courier services like DHL or local buses can deliver. Always insure valuable pieces.

Exhibitions are powerful. Apply to group shows at community centers, art fairs, and biennials. Prepare a artist statement (100 words) and a price list. At the exhibition, bring business cards and a guest book. Talk to visitors about your process. Offer prints or postcards as affordable alternatives. If you cannot afford a solo show, organize a pop-up in a friend's shop or at a market. In Lagos, the Lekki Arts & Crafts Market is a good starting point.

When selling, provide a certificate of authenticity. Include your name, title, date, medium, and dimensions. Package the artwork professionally. For local sales, hand-deliver if possible. For online sales, communicate clearly and ship promptly. Ask buyers for feedback and testimonials. Repeat customers and referrals are key. Finally, keep records of all sales for tax and inventory. With consistent effort, you can build a sustainable income from your charcoal art.

lessons.title: Archival Storage
lessons.body:
Archival storage keeps your charcoal drawings safe for decades. The enemies are light, heat, moisture, insects, and acid. Store your drawings in a cool, dark place with stable temperature (18-22Â°C) and humidity (45-55%). In tropical Africa, use a dehumidifier or silica gel packets in storage boxes. Avoid attics, basements, and garages. A closet in a living space is often better.

Use acid-free materials. Buy archival boxes, folders, or portfolios made of polypropylene or polyethylene. Do not use PVC plastic, which releases harmful gases. Interleave drawings with acid-free glassine or tissue paper. If you cannot find glassine, use unprinted newsprint, but change it every 6 months. Stack drawings flat, not rolled, to prevent curling. For large drawings, use a flat file cabinet with shallow drawers. Label each folder with the title, date, and medium.

Handle drawings with clean, dry hands or cotton gloves. Oils from your skin can damage charcoal. Support the drawing from underneath when moving it. Never touch the surface. If a drawing gets dusty, gently brush it with a soft, clean paintbrush. Do not use water or solvents. For framed pieces, keep them hanging away from direct sun and heat sources. Rotate your display every 3-6 months to limit light exposure.

Check your stored art every 3 months. Look for signs of mold, foxing, or insect damage. If you see mold, isolate the drawing and consult a conservator. For minor insect damage, freeze the drawing in a sealed plastic bag for 72 hours (if the drawing is not framed). This kills larvae. After freezing, let it return to room temperature before opening. Keep a inventory list with photos and locations. Digitize your collection by scanning or photographing each piece. Store digital copies on a cloud drive or external hard drive. This ensures your legacy even if physical pieces are lost.

lessons.title: Final Project: Complete Charcoal Artwork
lessons.body:
For your final project, you will create a finished charcoal artwork from start to finish, applying all the skills from this course. Choose a subject that reflects your African heritageâa market scene, a wildlife portrait, a traditional mask, or a landscape. Work on A3 (30x42 cm) or larger paper. Use a mix of charcoal types: willow for sketching, compressed for dark tones, and white charcoal for highlights. Plan your composition with a light pencil sketch, then build up layers of charcoal. Remember to use fixative between layers to prevent smudging.

Once the drawing is complete, fix it with 2-3 coats of workable fixative. Let it dry completely. Then mat and frame it using acid-free materials. Cut a mat with a 2 cm border around the drawing. Use a simple wooden frame that complements the artwork. Attach hanging hardware. Photograph the finished piece under natural light, using a tripod and editing for accuracy. Write a short artist statement (100 words) describing your inspiration and process.

Present your artwork to the class or online. Prepare a 5-minute talk: explain your subject, the charcoal types you used, and the challenges you faced. Show your before-and-after photos. Offer the piece for sale or display it in a local venue. Price it based on materials plus your time. For example, if you spent 10 hours at $10/hour and materials cost $20, price at $120. Include a certificate of authenticity.

Finally, store a digital copy and a physical portfolio of your project. Reflect on what you learned: fixing, framing, photographing, selling, and storing. This project is your portfolio piece to show potential clients or galleries. Take pride in your workâcharcoal art from Africa is unique and valuable. With these skills, you can turn your passion into a sustainable craft. Submit your project with photos, artist statement, and a short report on your process. Congratulations on completing the course!

quiz.q: What is the recommended distance to hold a fixative spray from a charcoal drawing?
quiz.explanation: Holding the can 30 cm away ensures an even coat without oversaturation.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a workable fixative brand mentioned in the lesson?
quiz.explanation: Krylon Workable Fixatif is a common brand for fixing charcoal.

quiz.q: What can you use as a cheaper alternative to fixative, but with caution?
quiz.explanation: Hairspray can work but may yellow over time, so test first.

quiz.q: How long should you wait between coats of fixative?
quiz.explanation: Waiting 10 minutes allows the previous coat to dry.

quiz.q: What is glassine paper used for?
quiz.explanation: Glassine is an acid-free paper placed over drawings to prevent smudging.

quiz.q: In humid regions, what should you add to storage boxes to prevent mold?
quiz.explanation: Silica gel absorbs moisture and prevents mold growth.

quiz.q: What is the recommended overlap of a mat over a drawing on each side?
quiz.explanation: A 2 cm overlap holds the drawing securely without covering too much.

quiz.q: Why should you hinge a drawing only at the top edge?
options: A) To allow paper to expand and contract
C) To make it easier to remove
quiz.explanation: Hinging at the top allows the paper to move with humidity changes.

quiz.q: Which glazing is lighter and safer for shipping but can scratch easily?
quiz.explanation: Acrylic (Plexiglas) is lighter and safer but scratches easily.

quiz.q: What should you use to seal the back of a frame to keep out dust and insects?
options: A) Kraft paper or framing tape
quiz.explanation: Kraft paper or framing tape creates a dust barrier.

quiz.q: Where can you find affordable wooden frames in Lagos?
quiz.explanation: Balogun Market in Lagos is known for affordable frames.

quiz.q: What is the ideal lighting for photographing charcoal art?
options: B) Natural daylight on a cloudy day
quiz.explanation: Cloudy daylight provides soft, even lighting without harsh shadows.

quiz.q: What should you do if your drawing is framed behind glass when photographing?
options: B) Remove it from the frame
quiz.explanation: Removing the drawing from the frame avoids reflections and glare.

quiz.q: Which app is recommended for editing photos of charcoal art?
quiz.explanation: Snapseed is a free photo editing app mentioned in the lesson.

quiz.q: What resolution should you use for printing reproductions?
quiz.explanation: 300 dpi is standard for high-quality printing.

quiz.q: What is a typical commission range for a gallery selling your art on consignment?
quiz.explanation: Galleries often take 30-50% commission.

quiz.q: What should you include in a certificate of authenticity?
options: A) Your name, title, date, medium, dimensions
quiz.explanation: A certificate of authenticity documents the artwork's details.

quiz.q: Which online platform is suggested for selling art?
quiz.explanation: Etsy is a popular marketplace for selling handmade art.

quiz.q: What is a good way to start exhibiting if you cannot afford a solo show?
options: A) Organize a pop-up in a friend's shop
B) Wait for a gallery to call
quiz.explanation: Pop-up exhibitions in local shops are low-cost and effective.

quiz.q: What should you keep records of for tax and inventory?
quiz.explanation: Keeping sales records is important for tax and inventory management.

quiz.q: What is the ideal temperature range for archival storage?
quiz.explanation: 18-22Â°C is a stable, cool temperature for storing art.

quiz.q: Which material should you avoid for storage because it releases harmful gases?
quiz.explanation: PVC plastic releases harmful gases that can damage art.

quiz.q: How often should you change unprinted newsprint used as interleaving?
quiz.explanation: Newsprint can become acidic, so change it every 6 months.

quiz.q: What should you do if you find mold on a stored drawing?
options: A) Isolate it and consult a conservator
quiz.explanation: Mold can spread, so isolate the piece and seek professional advice.

quiz.q: How long should you freeze a drawing to kill insect larvae?
quiz.explanation: Freezing for 72 hours kills most insect larvae.

quiz.q: What is the recommended size for the final project?
quiz.explanation: A3 (30x42 cm) or larger allows for detailed work.

quiz.q: Which charcoal type is used for sketching in the final project?
quiz.explanation: Willow charcoal is soft and ideal for initial sketches.

quiz.q: What should you include in your artist statement?
quiz.explanation: An artist statement describes your inspiration and creative process.

quiz.q: How should you price your final project?
options: A) Materials plus time at a fair hourly rate
quiz.explanation: Pricing should cover materials and compensate your time.

quiz.q: What is the final step after completing your final project?
options: A) Store a digital copy and physical portfolio
C) Give it away for free
quiz.explanation: Keeping digital and physical copies preserves your work for future opportunities.
